c.tagline: Morocco's sun-soaked Atlantic beach resort, rebuilt bold after the 1960 quake.

taxi.fareNote: Small orange 'petits taxis' work within the city and are metered — insist on the meter (compteur) or agree a price first, and expect to share the cab with other riders. Larger white 'grands taxis' cover longer and airport runs at a negotiated flat rate. Ride-hailing apps (Careem, inDrive, Yassir) operate but availability is limited and informal.

emergency.note: Dial 19 for police and 15 for ambulance/fire; 112 also works from mobiles. Tourist police patrol the beach promenade and main visitor areas.

avoid.reason: Petty crime on the beach and at night; hustlers

hood_desc: The lively city-center strip running behind the long crescent beach and its palm-lined promenade, packed with hotels, cafes, sunset bars, and restaurants; the most convenient, walkable base for first-timers who want the sand, dining, and nightlife on their doorstep.

A polished, modern yacht-harbour quarter at the north end of the bay with smart apartments, seafood terraces, cafes, and a clean promenade; suits design-conscious travelers wanting a calm, chic-but-central spot by the water.

An upscale resort belt of large all-inclusive hotels set in landscaped grounds along a calmer stretch of beach south of the center; ideal for families and switch-off holidays focused on pools and sand.

The historic, more local quarter on the hill above the center, rebuilt after the 1960 earthquake, with Olhão Garden, the Lebanon Mosque, budget hotels, and easy reach of the Souk El Had; suits travelers wanting Moroccan character and value.

A former fishing village north of the center where beach life mixes with local culture, known for its surf-friendly waves and laid-back guesthouses and surf camps; suits surfers and travelers seeking a quieter, more authentic base.

water.note: Tap water is chlorinated but most visitors stick to bottled.

transit.hours: Alsa city buses run roughly 6am to 10pm; there is no night service, so petits taxis fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Agadir has no metro or tram; the city is served by the Alsa bus network, but most visitors get around the compact beachfront and center on foot and by metered orange petits taxis.
transit.pay: Pay the bus fare in cash to the driver, around 4-5 MAD (~US$0.45) per ride; there is no rechargeable transit card worth buying for a short visit, so carry small change. Petits taxis are metered and inexpensive.

transit.m: Alsa city bus line to the center (~45-60 min, limited frequency)
Grand taxi to the city center (30-40 min; agree the fare first)

tip.r: ~5-10% at restaurants for good service; rounding up for taxis and a few dirhams for porters and café staff is customary.

food.name: Grilled sardines
food.desc: Agadir lands some of the world's biggest sardine catches. They are salted, flame-grilled whole and eaten with bread, cumin and lemon.

places.name: Port de Peche grill stalls
places.note: Pick your fish at the counter and it is grilled on the spot for a few dirhams.

places.name: Souk El Had food stalls
places.note: Morocco's largest market; simple grills serving locals all day long.

places.name: Le Parasol Bleu
places.note: Beach terrace known for fresh fish and seafood with sunset views.

food.name: Fish chermoula
food.desc: Local catch marinated in cilantro, garlic, paprika, cumin and lemon, then grilled over charcoal and served with bread and simple salads.

places.name: Port de Peche grill stalls
places.note: The most honest version, cooked minutes from the boats.

places.name: La Scala
places.note: Long-time favourite blending Mediterranean and Moroccan cooking; strong on fish.

places.name: Pure Passion
places.note: Marina-side kitchen that appears on most Agadir best-of lists.

food.name: Seafood tagine
food.desc: Agadir's coastal take on the national dish: fish, shrimp or squid slow-cooked in a clay cone with preserved lemon, olives, tomato and herbs.

places.name: La Scala
places.note: Reliable, long-established address for seafood tagine and grills.

places.name: Le Jardin d'Eau
places.note: Garden setting with a Moroccan and European menu; popular for tagines.

places.name: Pure Passion
places.note: Modern Moroccan cooking with a strong seafood focus by the water.

food.name: Couscous
food.desc: Steamed semolina piled with seven vegetables and lamb or chicken, traditionally the Friday family meal across Morocco.

places.name: Souk El Had food stalls
places.note: Small eateries serve the Friday couscous to market traders and locals.

places.name: Le Jardin d'Eau
places.note: Calm garden dining room with a full Moroccan menu including couscous.

places.name: La Scala
places.note: Dependable sit-down couscous if you want it outside Friday.

food.name: Harira
food.desc: Thick tomato, lentil and chickpea soup finished with fresh herbs and lemon. Eaten as a cheap standing breakfast or supper starter.

places.name: Souk El Had food stalls
places.note: Bowls served all day at market counters for a couple of dirhams.

places.name: Talborjt evening food stalls
places.note: Old-town district where locals eat harira with dates after dark.

places.name: Herguita
places.note: Promenade cafe-restaurant popular for Moroccan breakfasts and soups.

food.name: Amlou with msemen
food.desc: Souss-region spread of roasted almonds, argan oil and honey, scooped up with warm flaky msemen flatbread at breakfast.

places.name: Souk El Had argan stalls
places.note: Women's cooperatives sell amlou and argan oil beside the msemen griddles.

places.name: Herguita
places.note: Easy sit-down Moroccan breakfast with amlou, msemen and honey.

places.name: Argan cooperatives on the Taghazout road
places.note: Roadside cooperatives let you taste amlou where the argan is pressed.

food.name: Moroccan mint tea
food.desc: Gunpowder green tea steeped with spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from height into small glasses. Offered everywhere, all day.

places.name: Souk El Had tea stalls
places.note: Sip mint tea between stalls while bargaining; the local ritual.

places.name: Cafes on Boulevard Hassan II
places.note: Classic pavement cafes where Agadirois linger over tea for hours.

places.name: Marina d'Agadir cafes
places.note: Waterside terraces pouring mint tea with harbour views.

food.name: Fresh orange and almond juice
food.desc: Souss oranges pressed to order, plus creamy jus d'amande - almond milk blended with sugar and orange-flower water. Both alcohol-free.

places.name: Souk El Had juice stalls
places.note: Rows of presses serving orange, avocado and almond juices very cheaply.

places.name: Talborjt juice kiosks
places.note: Neighbourhood kiosks where locals stop for a glass on the walk home.

places.name: Marina d'Agadir cafes
places.note: Fresh-squeezed juices served on the promenade terraces.

landmarks: Agadir Oufella (Kasbah)
The hilltop ramparts of a 1540 fortress that survived the 1960 earthquake, reached by cable car for sublime views over the bay and marina.
Agadir Beach and Promenade
Ten kilometres of broad golden sand and a palm-lined corniche, the sun-drenched centrepiece of Morocco's premier seaside resort.
Souk El Had
One of Morocco's largest markets, a walled labyrinth of some 6,000 stalls piled with argan oil, spices, ceramics, and mountains of produce.
Marina d'Agadir
A chic Moorish-styled yacht harbour lined with cafes and boutiques, the departure point for boat trips and the promenade's most polished stretch.
Musee du Patrimoine Amazigh (Amazigh Heritage Museum)
A compact treasury of Berber culture displaying silver jewellery, carpets, and manuscripts that illuminate the Souss region's indigenous heritage.
Vallee des Oiseaux
A shady ribbon of aviaries and gardens threading through downtown, where flamingos, peacocks, and mouflon delight families escaping the beach heat.
Crocoparc
Lush botanical gardens on the city's edge slithering with over 300 Nile crocodiles, plus giant tortoises, iguanas, and anacondas.
La Medina d'Agadir (Medina Polizzi)
An artisan-built recreation of the earthquake-destroyed medina, its stone alleys and workshops crafted using traditional Berber techniques by designer Coco Polizzi.
Paradise Valley
A day-trip oasis in the High Atlas foothills where palm-shaded turquoise rock pools invite cliff-jumping and lazy swims in a biosphere reserve.
Taghazout
Morocco's laid-back surf capital just up the coast, a whitewashed fishing village turned board-riders' mecca with legendary point breaks like Anchor Point.

train.note: Agadir has no railway - ONCF's network ends at Marrakech, about three hours north, and the long-planned extension south has not been built. Supratours runs coaches timed to connect with the trains at Marrakech, sold as a through ticket. Otherwise fly into Agadir-Al Massira airport.

bus.note: Supratours (https://www.supratours.ma/) is the useful operator here because its coaches connect with ONCF trains at Marrakech on a single ticket, taking about 3 hours to Marrakech and continuing to Essaouira and Laayoune. CTM covers the same routes plus the long international runs to Europe via the Tanger Med ferry. Book online or at the terminals.

ferry.note: Agadir's port is a fishing and cargo harbour with no scheduled passenger ferry - the Canary Islands service that once ran from here has not operated for years. Morocco's crossings to Spain are all in the far north.

half.name: Taroudant
half.blurb: Walled market town ringed by red-mud ramparts, nicknamed Little Marrakech for its souks and traditional atmosphere.

half.name: Tiznit
half.blurb: Southern town known for its silversmiths and one of Morocco's largest jewelry souks, set behind red pisé walls.

half.name: Souss-Massa National Park
half.blurb: Coastal nature reserve near the Massa estuary protecting rare birds including the endangered northern bald ibis.

full.name: Marrakech
full.blurb: Morocco's most famous imperial city, with its bustling Jemaa el-Fnaa square, souks, and Islamic architecture, a few hours inland.
